_readme: Narrative text: activity-feed beats, per-biome line pools, biome lore stages (narrative.ts, lore.ts), and the four bookshelf stories (stories.ts). Line pools are JSON arrays. Keys are referenced as narrative.<key>.

kind.insect: The air over {biome} hums and ticks again — three kinds of insect have found their way back.
kind.bird: Birdsong has returned to {biome}; three species now forage and nest there.
kind.mammal: Trails wind through {biome} again — three kinds of mammal move through it now.
kind.amphibian: Frogs and salamanders are back in {biome} — a sure sign its water and damp ground are healthy.
kind.reptile: Reptiles bask in {biome} once more, now that there's warmth and cover to find.
kind.fish: The waters of {biome} hold fish again.
kind.invertebrate: The tidepools and shallows of {biome} are crowded with small life again.

allkinds: Every kind of creature — from the smallest insect to the top predator — is represented in {biome} now. A complete community.

combo.meadow-fox-prey: Fox and prey are both back in Willow Meadow. Predators like foxes keep rodent and rabbit numbers in check — which stops overgrazing and actually keeps the meadow more diverse, not less.
combo.meadow-hawk-rodent: A red-tailed hawk now hunts the meadow's rodents — nature's pest control. A single hawk can eat hundreds of mice and voles in a year.
combo.forest-owl-prey: The great horned owl hunts these woods after dark. Owls have offset ear openings that let them pinpoint a mouse in total blackness by sound alone.
combo.forest-bobcat-prey: A bobcat stalks Old Hollow Forest again — an ambush hunter that needs dense cover to creep close, which is exactly the understory you rebuilt.
combo.forest-cavity-reuse: A woodpecker carved a cavity, used it once, and left it — and another animal has moved straight in. In a forest, one bird's old home is another's new one.
combo.wetland-beaver: The beaver is back — an ecosystem engineer. Its dams raise the water table and flood new ponds, building habitat that fish, frogs, and birds all depend on.
combo.wetland-beaver-wake: Otters and herons have followed the beaver in. They hunt the deep, still water its dams create — habitat that simply wouldn't exist without it.
combo.wetland-heron-hunt: A great blue heron works the shallows. It hunts by standing utterly still for minutes, then striking faster than the eye can follow.
combo.desert-snake-rodent: The rattlesnake is back, and it earns its keep: an ambush hunter that senses prey by body heat through pits on its face, keeping desert rodent numbers down.
combo.desert-coyote-prey: A mountain-lion ranges the scrubland again — a generalist that hunts rodents and rabbits and, in doing so, keeps the whole desert food web balanced.
combo.desert-shared-burrow: Nobody wastes a hole in the desert: the tortoise digs a burrow, and a burrowing owl moves into the spare room. A few feet down, it's cool while the surface bakes.
combo.alpine-eagle-prey: A golden eagle patrols the ridge. It can spot a yellow-bellied-marmot from over a mile off and stoop at more than 150 mph — the high country's apex hunter.
combo.coastal-keystone: The ochre sea star is back — the original "keystone species." Remove it and mussels take over every rock; return it and the whole tidepool shares the space again.
combo.coastal-otter-kelp: An otter rafting offshore means a forest beneath it: otters eat the urchins that would otherwise graze the kelp down to bare rock.

total.total-10: Ten kinds of animal now share the preserve. What started as bare ground is starting to feel alive.
total.total-25: Twenty-five species across the preserve — the quiet you inherited has well and truly broken.
total.total-40: Forty kinds of neighbor now. Word has clearly travelled: this is a safe place again.

health.25: {biome} has crossed a quarter restored — bare ground is becoming real habitat, and the first hardy species can finally risk it.
health.50: {biome} is halfway back — and halfway is the tipping point. From here recovery speeds up, as the life you've brought back helps bring back more.
health.80: {biome} is thriving at 80% — healthy enough now to support its top predators and a full, working food web.
health.100: {biome} is fully restored. What you inherited as damaged ground is, simply, wild again.

meadow: Wind moves through the grass in long silver waves; somewhere a sparrow answers it.
The meadow smells of warm earth and crushed clover after you turn the soil.
Grasshoppers spring out of the grass ahead of your steps like little sparks.
Seed heads nod on their stalks, scattering next year's meadow on the breeze.
Dew beads the spiderwebs strung between the grass blades at first light.
A breath of wind carries dandelion seeds drifting past like tiny parachutes.
The light goes gold and low across the grass tips toward evening.
Crickets tune up in the warm grass — a sound you feel as much as hear.
Morning fog catches in the grass and burns off in ribbons as the sun climbs.
A meadow is never truly silent; even at night the crickets keep the conversation going.
Native grasses send roots three times deeper than the grass is tall — that's where a meadow stores its strength.
Grasslands hide most of their carbon underground, which is why a healthy meadow shrugs off fire and drought.
Wildflowers and pollinators evolved together; a flower's shape often matches the tongue of its favorite bee.
Ground-nesting birds rely on unmowed grass for cover — a tidy lawn is a desert to them.
Voles tunnel runways through the grass thatch, and those runways feed nearly every meadow predator.
Many meadow flowers bloom in sequence through the season, so something is always feeding the bees.
Clover pulls nitrogen out of the air and into the soil, quietly fertilizing the whole meadow for free.
Crab spiders hide inside flowers, perfectly camouflaged, ambushing the pollinators that visit.
Goldfinches wait to nest until thistles go to seed, timing their chicks to the food supply.
A single square foot of healthy meadow soil can hold more living things than there are people on Earth.
A grasshopper can leap 20 times its body length — like you clearing a bus from a standing start.
Ladybugs can eat 5,000 aphids in a lifetime, which is why gardeners adore them.
Monarch caterpillars eat only milkweed, storing its toxins to make themselves taste terrible.
A bumblebee's buzz isn't its wings — it's the flight muscles shivering to shake pollen loose.
Killdeer fake a broken wing to lure predators from the nest, then "recover" and fly off.
Butterflies taste with their feet before they decide to feed.
Crickets chirp faster when it's warmer — count the chirps and you can estimate the temperature.
A meadowlark isn't a lark at all, but a cousin of the blackbird with a flutelike song.
A single dandelion can launch 2,000 seeds, each on its own tiny parachute.
Bluebirds can spot a caterpillar in the grass from fifty feet away.
Swallows drink on the wing, skimming low to sip from puddles without ever landing.
Garter snakes are harmless to you and a quiet menace to the slugs and mice you'd rather not host.
Bees pollinate the flowers and the flowers feed the bees' young — neither would last long without the other.
Where the fox hunts, the rabbits stay on the move, and the grass they don't overgraze grows back thick.
The hawk overhead and the snake in the grass hunt the same voles from opposite directions.
The monarchs go where the milkweed grows, and the milkweed spreads wherever the meadow is left wild.
Rabbits crop the grass low in patches, and ground-feeding birds love the open lanes they leave behind.
Sparrows and finches eat the seeds the meadow drops, then scatter what they don't digest — gardeners with wings.
The first real flush of wildflowers has opened; color is returning to the meadow.
The bare patches are knitting closed — green is winning back the dust.
Butterflies are everywhere now; the meadow has hit its stride.
The meadow hums in a way it didn't when you arrived — that low insect drone is the sound of health.
Swallows work the bugs above the grass at dusk; hard to believe this was bare dirt.
The whir you hear at dusk is a nighthawk, mouth open, hoovering insects from the air.
Praying mantises are the meadow's tigers in miniature, ambushing insects far larger than themselves.
Leafcutter bees snip neat circles from leaves to line their nests, one tidy parcel at a time.
A patch of bare ground left in the sun becomes a runway and a sunning spot for ground bees and lizards.
Foxes have whiskers on their legs as well as their faces, feeling their way through the tall grass.
The deeper a meadow's roots, the more rain it drinks before a drop ever runs off.
Painted ladies are among the farthest-traveling butterflies on Earth, crossing whole continents.
By late summer the meadow is mostly seed — a banquet laid out for every bird that passes.
Fox on the ground and hawk in the air — the meadow's voles are hunted from both worlds now.
Butterflies, bees, and beetles all working the same blooms — the pollination crew is complete.
An owl has claimed the night shift over the meadow, hunting the mice the day birds never see.
Deer and rabbits graze the same grass at different heights, and between them keep it from running wild.
A berry bush beside a shrub: a pantry and a place to bolt for cover, exactly what the small birds want.
Wildflower patch and pollinator garden together have turned this corner into a bee highway.
Brush pile and rock pile both down — cover now for everything from voles to garter snakes.
Oak and willow both rooted, and the meadow finally has real shade to offer.
A pond to drink from and a bath to splash in — the meadow's birds have both now.
forest: Light falls in green shafts through the canopy, shifting as the leaves move.
The forest floor is springy underfoot — centuries of fallen leaves turned to soil.
Somewhere above, a woodpecker drums a hollow trunk like a knock at a door.
The air here is cool and damp and smells of moss and old wood.
A branch creaks; a squirrel scolds; then the forest settles back into its hush.
Mist hangs low between the trunks in the early morning, slow to lift under the canopy.
Mushrooms have pushed up overnight along a fallen log, pale against the dark wood.
Leaves spiral down one at a time, each a slow green-gold parachute.
A wren's song spills out of the understory, far bigger than the bird that made it.
Rain doesn't fall so much as drip here, handed down leaf by leaf from the canopy.
Dead standing trees, called snags, are some of the richest habitat in a forest — homes carved and reused for generations.
An old forest grows in layers — floor, understory, canopy — and each shelters a different community.
Beneath the soil, fungi link tree roots into networks that trade water and nutrients between trees.
A rotting log is not waste; it's a slow-release pantry feeding insects, fungi, newts, and the soil itself.
Mature trees pull water up from deep underground and breathe it into the air, making their own weather.
Forest soils store enormous amounts of carbon — disturb them and much of it escapes to the sky.
Many forest seeds need an animal to bury or carry them; the forest plants itself through its residents.
Owls fly almost silently thanks to comb-like feather edges that break up the sound of the air.
Bats can eat their own body weight in insects in a single night.
Salamanders breathe partly through their skin and need the damp, shaded forest floor to survive.
Flying squirrels don't truly fly — they glide on a membrane between their limbs, steering with the tail.
A pileated woodpecker can chisel a hole big enough to put your fist through, hunting carpenter ants.
Banana slugs can be bright yellow and as long as your hand, and they clean the forest floor as they go.
Black bears climb trees to nap on branches, sometimes wedged in surprisingly comfortably.
A chickadee's "dee-dee-dee" call adds more "dees" the more dangerous the predator it spots.
Newts can be toxic enough to make a predator deeply regret the attempt.
Squirrels sometimes "fake bury" nuts to fool any thieves watching them.
A bear's sense of smell is thousands of times keener than ours — it can wind food from miles off.
Wood ducks nest in tree cavities, and their ducklings leap from the hole to the ground on their first day.
Some forest fungi glow faintly in the dark — "foxfire" that early travelers used to mark trails.
A woodpecker carves a cavity, uses it once, and leaves it — and the forest's renters move straight in.
The owl hunts the night shift, the hawk the day — between them, few mice go uncounted.
Squirrels bury more nuts than they ever dig up, and the ones they forget grow into the next forest.
A bobcat needs dense cover to creep close — exactly the understory you've coaxed back.
Bats and owls split the night between insects and mice, and the forest is quieter for prey by dawn.
Saplings are catching hold in the open ground; the understory is finding its feet.
The canopy is starting to close overhead, and the floor below it cools into real forest.
Three layers of forest now — floor, understory, canopy — each with its own residents.
The woods feel old again, the kind of quiet that takes decades to grow back.
Moss holds rainwater like a sponge, releasing it slowly so the forest floor never quite dries.
A single oak can support over 2,000 species across its life — a whole world in one tree.
Porcupines have around 30,000 quills, each tipped with tiny barbs.
Nuthatches walk headfirst down tree trunks, seeing insects the upward-climbers miss.
Deadwood left to rot returns more to the forest than living wood ever could.
Fishers are one of the few hunters quick enough to flip a porcupine and take it safely.
Tree rings record droughts, fires, and good years alike — a diary written in wood.
The understory shrubs feed the deer and the berries feed the birds; nothing in the layers goes spare.
A woodpecker's tongue is so long it wraps around the back of its skull when not in use.
Ravens mimic sounds, solve puzzles, and seem to slide and tumble through the air just for fun.
Fallen leaves shelter overwintering insects that become the first food of spring.
Spotted towhees rummage in the leaf litter so loudly you'd swear they were something far bigger.
A forest cools the air around it; step under the canopy on a hot day and you'll feel it drop.
Two owl species splitting the night between them — the forest dark is well hunted now.
The big woodpecker carves the holes and the wood ducks claim them — cavity housing, forest-style.
A large predator roams these woods again, and the whole forest is more alert for it.
Squirrels by day, flying squirrels by night — canopy and cavities both busy around the clock.
Standing deadwood and a nesting tree together: the woodpeckers carve, and everyone else moves in.
Mushroom log and hollow log both rotting down — fungi fed, newts sheltered, soil rebuilt.
A woodland pool beside a fern spring gives the salamanders the damp they can't live without.
A berry bush in the understory with ferns underfoot — food and cover on the forest floor at once.
wetland: Reeds rattle softly in the wind, and somewhere out in them a frog clears its throat.
The water lies still and dark, doubling the sky and the reeds along its edge.
A dragonfly stitches back and forth above the surface, all glittering wings.
Mud sucks at your boots near the bank, rich and black and full of life.
Concentric rings spread where something rose to feed, then vanished again.
The marsh smells green and mineral, of wet earth and growing reeds.
Red-winged blackbirds sway on the cattails, flashing their shoulders and calling.
Mist sits on the water at dawn until the first heron steps through it.
A water strider skates the surface tension, dimpling the water without breaking it.
Frogs go quiet as you pass, then start up again behind you, one brave voice at a time.
Wetlands filter pollutants and store floodwater — doing for free what costs cities millions.
Amphibians breathe partly through their skin, so their presence is a sign the water is clean.
A marsh is among the most productive habitats on Earth, rivaling rainforests for sheer abundance.
Reed beds are nurseries — countless young fish, frogs, and insects hide among the stems.
Wetlands recharge groundwater, letting rain soak in slowly instead of rushing away.
Cattails clean the water as they grow, drawing excess nutrients up into their stalks.
Many birds migrate thousands of miles between wetlands — lose one and a whole journey breaks.
Mud at the bottom of a marsh can lock away carbon for thousands of years.
Frogs' eggs, tadpoles, and adults each fill a different role in the food web as they grow.
Still water grows warm and rich; moving water stays cool and clear. A marsh needs both.
Dragonflies have hunted these skies for over 300 million years — older than the dinosaurs.
A dragonfly catches prey in midair over 90% of the time — one of nature's deadliest hunters.
Beavers' front teeth never stop growing; gnawing wood is what keeps them filed down.
Some turtles can breathe through their rear ends, handy for a winter spent underwater.
A heron's neck has a special hinge that lets it strike like a loosed spring.
Otters keep a favorite rock as a tool and tuck it in a "pocket" of loose skin.
Bitterns point their bills skyward and sway with the reeds to vanish in plain sight.
A bullfrog's call can carry half a mile across still water on a calm night.
Kingfishers hover, then dive headfirst, closing a third eyelid like goggles before they hit.
Muskrats build little lodges and push-up feeding huts out of the reeds they cut.
The beaver doesn't move into habitat — it builds it. Its dam makes the deep water everyone else needs.
Otters and herons both hunt the still water the beaver's dam holds back.
The heron stalks the shallows the frogs hide in, and the frogs eat the insects the reeds shelter.
Turtles bask on the logs that otters and muskrats leave drifting — everything gets reused here.
Where there are minnows there are kingfishers; the marsh feeds upward from the smallest fish.
Water is finding the old channels again, and the reeds are rising to meet it.
The marsh is loud now — frogs, blackbirds, the whir of dragonflies all at once.
Open water and reed bed and mud bank, all here at once: the marsh reads as a marsh again.
Standing at the water's edge, it's hard to picture the cracked mud you started from.
Sandhill cranes mate for life and dance to court — bowing, leaping, tossing grass in the air.
A wetland's edge, where water meets land, packs in more species than either side alone.
Leopard frogs can leap many times their length to vanish into the water at the first alarm.
Mergansers have serrated bills — "sawbills" — for gripping the slippery fish they chase underwater.
Cattail fluff was once used to stuff life jackets; the marsh has always been useful.
Damselflies fold their wings along their backs at rest; dragonflies hold theirs out flat.
A beaver pond slows the water enough for silt to settle, clearing everything downstream.
Marsh wrens build several dummy nests, leaving a predator to guess which one holds the eggs.
Green herons sometimes drop a feather or insect on the water as bait, then snatch the fish it draws.
Whirligig beetles have split eyes that watch above and below the waterline at the same time.
A single acre of healthy marsh can shelter thousands of nesting and migrating birds in a season.
Cattail roots were a staple food here long before there were towns to drain the marsh.
Beaver and otter both working the water — the marsh has its engineer and its acrobat.
Heron in the shallows, fish in the water below it — the marsh's food chain is wired together.
A tall marsh bird stalks the reeds again, patient as the water itself.
Turtles share the basking logs by day; nothing here wastes a sunny perch.
Reed bed and cattail stand together: nursery and cover for half the marsh at once.
A lily pool above a mud bank — frogs get sun and ooze both, just how they like it.
A nesting platform over the water and logs to bask on — marsh birds and turtles both set.
Bulrush and sedge tussocks give the marsh wrens a whole maze to hide their nests in.
desert: Heat shimmers off the flats, and the only sound is the wind moving sand grain by grain.
A roadrunner darts between the brush, all legs and purpose, and is gone.
The light is huge here, and the shadows under each shrub are sharp and cool.
Come dusk the desert exhales; the heat lifts and the night shift begins to stir.
A lizard does push-ups on a warm stone, claiming the rock for itself.
The brush smells of dust and resin, sharpened by the heat.
Stars come out thick and close over the desert once the sun is finally down.
Tracks cross the sand from the night before — a story of who went where in the cool dark.
A cactus wren rattles from a cholla, scolding nothing in particular.
After a rare rain the whole flat turns faintly green, racing to bloom before it dries.
Many desert animals never drink — they wring water from the seeds they eat and their own metabolism.
Burrows are the desert's air-conditioning: a few feet down it stays mild while the surface bakes.
Cactus opens its pores at night, not in the daytime heat, to lose as little water as it can.
Desert soil wears a living crust of moss and lichen that holds it together — one footstep can undo years.
Seeds can wait years in the desert soil for the one good rain that makes blooming worth it.
Shade is a resource here; a single nurse plant can shelter a dozen seedlings beneath it.
Desert predators hunt at dawn and dusk to dodge both the heat and the cold of deep night.
A saguaro can take 50 years to grow its first arm and live for over 150.
Pack rats build middens that, preserved in the dry air, can record the desert's history for millennia.
The desert runs on pulses — long waits broken by sudden, frantic abundance after rain.
Kangaroo rats can go their whole lives without drinking a drop of water.
A horned lizard can squirt a jet of blood from its eyes to startle a predator.
Roadrunners can sprint over 20 mph and would genuinely rather run than fly.
Elf owls are smaller than a soda can and nest in holes woodpeckers leave in the cactus.
Tarantulas can go months between meals and live for decades.
A Gila woodpecker drills nest holes in saguaros that countless other desert animals later use.
Jackrabbits dump heat through their enormous ears, which glow with blood vessels.
Some desert toads sleep underground for most of the year, surfacing only for the rains.
Chuckwallas wedge into rock cracks and puff up so tightly that nothing can pull them out.
A kit fox's huge ears dump heat and pick up the faintest rustle of a beetle in the dark.
Nobody wastes a hole in the desert: the tortoise digs the burrow, the owl takes the spare room.
The rattlesnake senses prey by body heat and keeps the rodents in check — pest control with patience.
A mountain-lion eats whatever the desert offers, and in doing so keeps the whole web from tipping.
The woodpecker carves the cactus, and elf owls and flycatchers move into the holes it leaves.
Quail travel in coveys, dozens of eyes watching for the hawk so each can keep feeding.
Brush is taking hold, and with it the first scraps of shade the flat has had in years.
Burrows dot the ground now; the desert's life has somewhere to escape the sun.
Cactus, brush, and burrow all in place — the scrubland is functioning as a desert should.
At dusk the whole flat comes alive with rustles and calls; the dead heat is long gone.
Costa's hummingbirds dive-display in the desert spring, the sun flaring purple off their throats.
Agave may grow for decades, bloom once in a towering spike, and then die — all on one budget of water.
Antelope squirrels run with their tails flipped over their backs like little parasols.
A desert night can be 40 degrees cooler than the same spot at noon.
Phainopeplas eat mistletoe berries and plant the next crop wherever they perch.
Banded geckos squeak when grabbed and can drop their tail to make a clean escape.
Desert bees nest in the ground and time their whole lives to a few weeks of bloom.
Wash channels carry the rare flood, and the biggest brush always grows along their banks.
Creosote bushes can clone themselves for thousands of years from a single original plant.
Scorpions glow an eerie blue-green under ultraviolet light, for reasons no one fully understands.
Desert iguanas stay active at body temperatures that would kill most other lizards.
A sudden downpour can fill a bone-dry wash with a flash flood in a matter of minutes.
Tortoise burrow with a borrowed owl inside — desert real estate is fully booked.
Rattlesnake and kangaroo rat sharing the same flat — predator and prey, the desert in balance.
A desert hunter ranges the flats after dark now, reading the sand for tracks.
The woodpecker drills the cactus and the elf owl takes the hole — the saguaro is an apartment block.
A burrow mound and a shaded rock shelter give the desert two ways to duck the sun.
Cactus and brush together: shade, cover, and food where there used to be only bare flat.
Marigolds and a nectar feeder out — now the hummingbirds have a reason to detour through here.
Mesquite and palo verde, the desert's nurse trees, shading every seedling that starts beneath them.
alpine: The wind never quite stops up here; it leans on the grass and combs the snowfields.
Far below, the lower country lies hazed and small; up here the air is thin and bright.
A yellow-bellied-marmot's whistle bounces off the rock and the whole slope seems to listen.
Cloud shadows slide across the talus, and for a moment the mountain dims, then blazes again.
Snowmelt trickles between the stones, ice-cold and clear enough to see every pebble.
Cushion plants hug the ground in tight green mounds, out of the wind's reach.
The quiet up here has weight to it, broken only by wind and the odd falling stone.
Wildflowers crowd a sheltered hollow, blooming hard and fast in the short alpine summer.
Frost still rims the shadows at midday where the sun hasn't reached.
A pika dashes across the rocks with a mouthful of flowers, working against the coming winter.
Alpine plants grow low and slow against the cold — some cushion plants are centuries old but inches across.
Snow is insulation: many small animals spend winter in the mild gap between snowpack and ground.
Alpine soils are thin and ancient; a single inch can take a thousand years to form.
Up here, summer is a sprint — plants must sprout, flower, and seed in just a few frantic weeks.
Snowmelt timing sets the whole mountain's clock; everything blooms and breeds to match it.
Lichens grow on bare rock at a fraction of a millimeter a year, the slow pioneers of the heights.
Cold, clean meltwater holds more oxygen — which is why alpine trout can live in it.
Wind-stunted trees at treeline can be ancient, twisted into shapes by centuries of gales.
Alpine species are climate sentinels — as it warms they can only climb, until they run out of mountain.
A meadow of alpine wildflowers may bloom all at once, racing the snow that will return in weeks.
Pikas don't hibernate — they spend all summer stacking "haypiles" to eat under the snow.
A golden eagle can spot prey from over a mile away and stoop at more than 150 mph.
Mountain goats aren't true goats, and they scale near-vertical cliffs on rubbery, gripping hooves.
Ptarmigan grow feathered "snowshoes" on their feet and turn white to vanish in winter.
Clark's nutcrackers can hide tens of thousands of pine seeds and remember where most of them are.
Marmots spend up to eight months a year hibernating, hearts barely ticking over.
Bighorn rams crash heads at 20 mph; their skulls are built with a double layer to take it.
An ermine turns from brown to pure white in winter, keeping only a black tail-tip.
Rosy-finches nest higher than almost any other songbird, right up among the snowfields.
Snowshoe hares change coat color with the seasons, brown in summer and white in snow.
When the eagle circles, the marmots whistle and the whole slope freezes — the alarm that ties the heights together.
Clark's nutcracker plants the pines it forgets, and the whole treeline marches uphill on its memory.
Pikas and marmots share the talus, one stacking hay, the other sunning on the boulders above.
The ermine follows the voles into the gap beneath the snow, hunting where the cold can't reach.
Trout hold in the snowmelt pools, and the eagles and martens learn exactly where to watch.
Turf is knitting back over the bare talus, a fraction of an inch at a time.
Wildflowers have taken the sheltered hollows, and the marmots have someplace worth sunning.
Turf, snowmelt pool, and rocky shelter all in place — the high country is whole again.
An eagle could circle this ridge now and find a slope full of life beneath it.
Boreal toads climb surprisingly high, breeding in snowmelt ponds that vanish by late summer.
Mountain bluebirds hover like kestrels before dropping on insects in the turf.
Whitebark pines depend almost entirely on the nutcracker to plant their seeds.
Alpine air holds less oxygen, so the animals that live here run on famously efficient blood.
Pine grosbeaks are so unafraid of people that old-timers called them "mope-heads."
A yellow-bellied-marmot colony posts sentries; one whistle and every burrow empties in a heartbeat.
Snow lingers in the shadows of boulders into midsummer, watering the flowers downhill of it.
Up here, a warm rock in the morning sun is the most valuable real estate on the mountain.
Glacier lilies push up through the very edge of the melting snow to bloom before anything else.
White-crowned sparrows sing slightly different dialects from one mountain to the next.
Alpine chipmunks scatter their seed caches in dozens of hidden larders to outlast the winter.
The treeline isn't really a line — it's a slow surrender of forest to wind and cold.
Pika stacking hay and yellow-bellied-marmot sunning above it — the talus is fully tenanted now.
Eagle circling and marmots below to whistle the alarm — the whole slope works as one.
A cliff-climber has claimed the crags, picking its way where nothing else dares.
A small, fierce hunter works the talus now, slipping between the stones after voles.
Snowmelt pool beside alpine flowers — water and forage both, in the brief mountain summer.
Heather mat and moss cushion knitting the thin soil together against the wind.
Krummholz pine and subalpine fir holding the treeline — the last trees before the bare heights.
A burrow mound tucked into a rock pile — the pikas and marmots have their fortress.
coastal: The surf comes in long and steady, and the whole shore breathes with it.
Gulls wheel and squabble over the wrack line, picking through what the tide left behind.
The air is all salt and kelp and cold spray off the breakers.
A wave draws back and the tidepools brim, each a tiny world of color.
Sandpipers chase the retreating water and flee the next wave, over and over, never quite caught.
Fog rolls in off the water and softens the whole coast to grays and silver.
Sea glass and shell fragments glint where the last high tide stranded them.
The rocks are slick with weed and loud with the suck and hiss of the surge.
A brown-pelican glides a hand's breadth above the swell, riding the cushion of air it makes.
Out past the breakers, the sea heaves slow and enormous and indifferent.
Tidepool animals live a double life, surviving both crashing waves and hours of exposure to air.
Kelp can grow up to two feet a day, building underwater forests that shelter hundreds of species.
Dune grasses anchor the shore with deep roots — without them, one storm can wash a beach away.
The wrack line of stranded kelp feeds a whole community of insects, birds, and crabs.
Mussels and barnacles filter the seawater, clearing it as they feed.
A tidepool's residents are zoned by how long they can stand being out of water.
Estuaries and shorelines are nurseries for fish that later fill the open ocean.
Anemones sting their prey with harpoon cells too small to feel through your skin.
Eelgrass meadows lock away carbon faster, acre for acre, than a rainforest.
Migrating shorebirds time their stopovers to the tides, feeding on what the water uncovers.
Sea otters hold hands while they sleep so the current doesn't drift them apart.
A sea star can push its stomach out of its body to digest prey too big to swallow.
Hermit crabs trade up shells as they grow, sometimes lining up to swap in size order.
A group of pelicans is a "squadron," and they plunge-dive for fish from up to 60 feet.
Octopuses can taste with their arms and squeeze through any gap bigger than their beak.
Sea stars can regrow lost arms, and a few can regrow a whole body from one.
Sanderlings run on legs that blur like clockwork as they chase the waves.
A barnacle glues its own head to the rock and kicks food into its mouth with its legs.
Harbor seals can sleep underwater, surfacing to breathe without ever waking.
Gray whales make one of the longest migrations of any mammal — thousands of miles each way.
The sea star is the original keystone: remove it and mussels take every rock; return it and all share the space.
An otter offshore means a forest beneath it — it eats the urchins that would mow the kelp to stubble.
Pelicans and cormorants follow the fish the kelp shelters; the forest below feeds the wings above.
Oystercatchers pry open the mussels the tide grows fat, prizing the rocks open one by one.
Where the anemones and mussels share a rock in peace, you can thank the sea star patrolling it.
Dunes are anchoring and the tidepools are filling; the shore is finding its footing.
Crabs, anemones, gulls — the wrack line and the rocks are busy again.
Anchored dune, full tidepool, kelp in the wrack: the whole shore is working as one.
Whale-spout to clam-siphon, the coast hums with life from the deep water to the dry sand.
Green sea turtles can hold their breath for hours while resting on the bottom.
A mussel anchors itself with "byssal threads" stronger, for their size, than steel cable.
Dolphins sleep one half of their brain at a time so they never stop surfacing to breathe.
Snowy plovers nest in bare scrapes on open sand, which is why a quiet beach matters so much.
Kelp holds onto rock with a "holdfast," not roots — it drinks straight from the seawater.
Turnstones flip stones and weed looking for the small life hiding underneath — hence the name.
Bat stars come in a riot of colors, no two quite the same.
The highest tides of the month come with the new and full moon, reaching places the sea rarely touches.
Anna's hummingbirds dive from on high and "sing" with their tail feathers in a courtship power-dive.
Pigeon guillemots flash bright red feet and mouths as they court along the sea cliffs.
A receding tide opens a whole world that will be underwater again within hours.
Beach hoppers bury themselves in damp sand by day and swarm the wrack line after dark.
Sea star patrolling the rock and anemones holding their space beneath it — the tidepool shares fairly now.
Otter and seal both offshore — the kelp beds are rich enough to feed them both.
Pelicans and cormorants diving the same shoals — the fish the kelp shelters feed the wings above.
Shorebirds work the open sand again, racing the waves for what the water uncovers.
Tidepool and kelp wrack together: the crabs and gulls have both a home and a buffet.
Dune grass and beach shrub anchoring the sand — the shore can hold a storm now.
Eelgrass and oyster beds filtering the shallows — the water clears and the fish come back.
Safe nesting ground above the tide line — the shorebirds can finally raise young here.

meadow.damaged: Bare, dusty ground where a flowering meadow used to be. With the native grasses gone, the pollinators left — and everything that ate them followed.
meadow.recovering: Grass and wildflower are knitting back in. Bees and butterflies work the new blooms, sparrows pick the seed, and the first hunters start watching the edges.
meadow.thriving: A meadow that hums. Voles tunnel the grass, hawks ride the thermals above them, and a fox can finally find enough to stay.
meadow.restored: A full grassland food web, top to bottom — pollinator to predator. Healthy meadows like this store carbon in their deep roots and feed a third of the preserve’s insects.
meadow.coexistence: The fox and the hawks only settle once the voles and rabbits are back — predators arrive last, when there’s finally enough prey to feed them.

forest.damaged: A logged-over woodland. The big trees and standing snags are gone, so the woodpeckers have nowhere to carve — and the cavity-nesters that reuse their holes never come.
forest.recovering: The understory is filling in: ferns, shrubs, deadwood for the newts. Squirrels and woodpeckers are back, and where there’s prey the first owls test the dark.
forest.thriving: Three layers of forest now — floor, understory, canopy — each with its own residents. Flying squirrels glide between the very trees you raised.
forest.restored: A full, layered old wood. Woodpeckers cut the homes; owls, ducks, and flying squirrels move into the holes they leave behind. Nothing in a forest is wasted.
forest.coexistence: One big woodpecker carves a cavity, uses it once, and abandons it — and a wood duck, a flying squirrel, or an owl moves straight in.

wetland.damaged: A drained marsh of cracked mud and dry channels. Without standing water, the whole chain — insects, fish, frogs, the birds that hunt them — has nowhere to begin.
wetland.recovering: Water is back in the channels and the reeds are rising. Frogs, dragonflies, and striders arrive first; herons follow the frogs into the shallows.
wetland.thriving: A loud, wet marsh. Otters and mink work the banks, turtles bask on the logs, and a beaver’s pond holds the whole place together.
wetland.restored: A complete wetland — crane to minnow. It filters everything downstream of it, quiet unpaid work that the whole watershed depends on.
wetland.coexistence: The beaver builds the habitat everyone else needs: its dam makes the deep, still water that otters hunt and herons stalk.

desert.damaged: An overgrazed flat with no brush and no burrows. With nowhere to escape the heat, even the hardiest animals stay away.
desert.recovering: Cactus and brush are taking hold, and the first burrows give shade a place to start. Kangaroo rats and lizards venture out at dusk.
desert.thriving: Life that knows how to wait out the sun. Tortoises dig, owls move into the spare burrows, and a mountain-lion can finally make a living here.
desert.restored: The hardest country in the preserve, fully alive — elf owl in the cactus, desert-tarantula under the stone. You can’t flood a desert back; you have to shade it back.
desert.coexistence: In the desert nobody wastes a hole — a tortoise digs a burrow and a burrowing owl moves into the spare room beneath the brush.

alpine.damaged: A trampled alpine slope, the wildflower turf worn through to bare talus. Up here recovery is measured in decades, not seasons.
alpine.recovering: Turf is knitting back over the rock. Pikas haul hay into the talus, marmots sun on the boulders, and rosy-finches work the snowmelt edges.
alpine.thriving: A living high country. Goats and bighorn pick the cliffs, trout hold in the snowmelt pools, and an eagle circles the ridge.
alpine.restored: The whole range restored against the wind — goat to white-tailed-ptarmigan to trout. Thin air, short summers, and yet a full web holds on up here.
alpine.coexistence: When the eagle circles the ridge, the marmots whistle and the whole slope goes still — the alarm that ties the high country together.

coastal.damaged: A scoured shore of washed-out dunes and empty tidepools. Without the anchoring dune grass and the kelp wrack, the tide has nothing to feed.
coastal.recovering: Dunes are anchoring and the tidepools are filling — crabs, anemones, mussels. Gulls and plovers work the wrack line again.
coastal.thriving: A living edge. Sea stars patrol the rock, otters raft offshore, and pelicans dive the surf where the fish have returned.
coastal.restored: The wildest stretch of the preserve, whole — whale-spout to clam-siphon. Two keystones do the quiet work that holds it all in balance.
coastal.coexistence: Two keystones run this shore: the sea star keeps mussels from taking every rock, and the otter eats the urchins that would otherwise mow down the kelp.

stories._readme: The four books on the home bookshelf (ui/stories.ts, ui/storyArt.tsx). Each book is four pages you turn one at a time; every page has a title, its text, and the captions under its picture — `figures` must stay the same length as that page's figure list in storyArt.tsx, in the same order. Plain explanation, no whimsy: these are the only place the game says outright what its systems are modelling.

1.title: Three jobs
1.text: An animal doesn't need a place so much as it needs a place that does three jobs: something to eat, somewhere to shelter, and water it can reach. Miss any one of the three and the other two don't count for much.

2.title: Close enough to matter
2.text: Distance matters as much as presence. Food has to be close enough to cover that a short dash gets an animal back under it. Water that can only be reached across open ground is water most small animals won't use.

3.title: Sharing a meadow
3.text: The place is the habitat. How an animal makes its living in it is the niche — what it eats, when it is active, what it keeps away from. Two species can share one meadow without competing, because one takes seed at dawn and the other hunts insects at dusk.

4.title: The piece that gets forgotten
4.text: This is why planting flowers alone rarely brings anything in. Cover is the piece most often missing. A brush pile or a hedgerow isn't decoration; for a rabbit or a wren it is the difference between passing through and staying.

1.title: Follow a fox backwards
1.text: Follow a fox backwards. It eats voles and ground-nesting birds. They eat insects and seed. The insects eat grass. The grass runs on sunlight. Four steps, and the fox depends on every one of them.

2.title: A tenth at every step
2.text: Only about a tenth of the energy at each step carries up to the next. The rest is spent staying alive. That ratio is why the numbers narrow so sharply toward the top: a meadow can support a great many grasshoppers, a good many sparrows, fewer voles, and one fox.

3.title: Last in, first out
3.text: So predators are the last to arrive and the first to go. They need every level beneath them filled before they can settle, and they feel a thinning at the bottom before anything else does.

4.title: What a fox tells you
figures: a meadow that can hold one
4.text: It also means a meadow with no hunters in it isn't a peaceful meadow, it's an incomplete one. When a fox does settle, what that tells you is that the levels underneath are carrying enough weight to hold it.

1.title: A beaver builds for itself
1.text: A beaver dams a creek because it wants water deep enough to swim in and stay out of reach. It isn't doing it for anything else. But the pond it makes is habitat that was not there before.

2.title: Everything that moves in
2.text: Still water gives frogs somewhere to lay eggs and dragonfly larvae somewhere to grow. The shallow edge gives a heron somewhere to fish. Trees that drown standing go soft and become nest sites for woodpeckers. One animal's construction turns into housing for a dozen species.

3.title: Engineers and keystones
3.text: An animal that reshapes the physical place like this is called an ecosystem engineer. A keystone species is related but different: it builds nothing, and holds the food web together far out of proportion to its numbers — sea otters keeping urchins off the kelp, wolves keeping elk off the riverbanks. Take one out and the whole system reorganises around the gap.

4.title: Why the next one is quicker
4.text: A few of both live here. When one of them comes back, the animals that depend on what it does tend to follow quickly, because the habitat they were waiting on has just been built for them.

1.title: Weeds first
1.text: Bare ground does not turn into woodland directly. Weeds and grasses arrive first, because they are the only things that can hold on there. They anchor the soil, shade it, and slow the water running off it.

2.title: What shrubs need
2.text: That changed ground is what shrubs need to establish. Shrubs add deeper roots, leaf litter and more shade, and only in the soil that makes will most tree seedlings survive their first few years. Each stage makes the next one possible and is then partly replaced by it.

3.title: A seedling isn't habitat
3.text: The sequence is called succession, and it runs on the plants' timescale rather than anyone else's. A seedling is not habitat yet. It has to grow in before it shades anything, feeds anything, or holds a nest.

4.title: Late, then quickly
4.text: Which is worth knowing during the stretch where a planted area looks like it is doing nothing. Roots are going down, water is being held in the ground longer, and seed is banking up in the soil. The visible change comes late, and then comes quickly.
